prize_parts.citation: For showing that liquid-liquid phase separation of multivalent biomolecules is a physical-chemical principle by which cells organise their contents

statement.case_for: I keep condensates as my preferred single part, but I have narrowed what I would reward. Hyman and Brangwynne showed that P granules and nucleoli behave as liquids that form, fuse and dissolve, and Rosen and colleagues showed with reconstituted multivalent systems that valency and interaction strength set phase boundaries and concentration thresholds. That is a general physical-chemical principle, tested quantitatively in vitro and in defined cellular systems, and it has changed how biochemistry, cell biology and neurodegeneration research describe intracellular organisation. It rests on thermodynamics and intermolecular forces, not on a technique. The round-1 exchange did not give me a reason to think another candidate has a more compact conceptual core. I would word the citation around the principle and not around function of every putative condensate in vivo, which is where the evidence is contested.
statement.case_against: The in vivo evidence is the real weakness, and Chabes and Linke both pressed it fairly. Many condensates were characterised by overexpression or in vitro demixing, and separating genuine phase separation from other assemblies at physiological concentrations is unresolved. Part of the physics descends from Flory-Huggins and coacervation theory, so novelty rests on the cellular demonstration and on the multivalency framework. The three-name cap excludes Pappu and Mittag, whose sequence-grammar work is serious. No other member preferred B026 in round 1, so it is far from five votes, and I am a soft-matter physical chemist who may overvalue a framework that resembles my own field. If the committee judges the in vivo question to be a maturity failure, my honest fallback is B011, with B034 behind it.

responses.point: Chabes argues that targeted protein degradation has a simpler experimental criterion than condensates (the target disappears and the ternary complex can be measured), and that evidence for phase separation in vivo at physiological concentrations rests too often on overexpression.
responses.response: The criticism of condensate evidence is fair, and it has changed my citation: I now credit the principle, supported by reconstitution and defined cellular systems, and not the claim that every observed body is a phase-separated functional compartment. I do not think the criterion of 'the target disappears' is a higher bar of chemistry than a phase diagram that can be measured, but it is a more easily certified one, and I accept that. My remaining hesitation on B034 is credit. Your trio includes Handa for cereblon, while Aili would leave him out, and either way Ciulli, Sakamoto, Kim and Gray are outside the cap. I would need the committee to settle whether the PROTAC concept and the glue mechanism are one achievement before I could place it above B026.

responses.point: Linke presses what exactly was discovered and when for condensates, notes that the credit among Hyman, Brangwynne, Rosen, Pappu and Mittag is unsettled, and calls the idea promising but premature compared with a routinely used method.
responses.response: I accept the first half. The discovery is the liquid-like behaviour of P granules and nucleoli in 2009 and 2011 and the multivalency framework in 2012, and I would keep the citation to that. I disagree that routine use is the right yardstick for a conceptual prize, since the concept is used daily in cell biology, soft matter and disease research even where individual cases are disputed. On your own configuration, my concern stands: reversible-terminator chemistry for B011 is defensible, but your nanopore part credits Bayley alone, and the chair's own summary says five members find that hard to defend. If B001 cannot be given a clean living set of names, I would rather you drop it and keep B011 on its own, which I could then support as an alternative.

responses.point: Brzezinski keeps Gray and Winkler on long-range protein electron transfer as a quantitative physical mechanism confirmed over three decades, and acknowledges that no one else ranked it.
responses.response: I still find B028 the most mature physical-chemical argument on the list, and the two-name credit is clean. My difficulty is that Dutton, Moser, Beratan and Onuchic made the picture quantitative, so the citation would honour a line of work with Marcus theory behind it, and the committee would have to explain why Gray and Winkler rather than the field. That is a smaller obstacle than for condensates on maturity, but a larger one on breadth. I am not moving it above B026, but I would support it as a second-choice part if you can show what Gray and Winkler established that Marcus theory plus the tunnelling-pathway work did not.

responses.point: Aqvist prefers the Balasubramanian and Klenerman pair for sequencing by synthesis, calls it a simple chemistry-driven game-changer with fully realised and independently confirmed consequences, and concedes the platform and Rothberg priority questions.
responses.response: This is the strongest mature candidate and the clean pair is its main advantage, so I keep B011 as my first alternative. I am glad you state the platform objection yourself, because it is the one I would put to anyone supporting it: the citation must reward reversible terminators with cleavable fluorophores on clustered molecules and not the sequencing field. If Rothberg's 454 priority is not settled by the expert reports, a two-name credit invites a challenge that the committee should anticipate. I would support it if condensates fall short.

uncertainties: Whether the committee treats the unresolved in vivo status of condensates as a failure of maturity or as a debate inside a mature concept.
Whether Rosen belongs with Hyman and Brangwynne, or whether Pappu or Mittag should take the third place for sequence grammar.
Whether the expert reports settle priority claims (Rothberg, Kosugi, Kondo and Nishida) that affect my alternatives B011 and others.
Whether B034 can be fixed as one citation, which determines whether I would place it above B011.
statement.conflict_note: My research on lipid and protein self-assembly is adjacent to biomolecular condensate work (B026), which I prefer, so I flag possible bias and would accept a recusal ruling on B026 if the committee wished. I share Lund University with Heiner Linke and Peter Somfai. I have no direct collaboration with any credited candidate that I am aware of.
